# The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents

Geyuan Wang Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University
Email: [geyuan001@e.ntu.edu.sg](mailto:)    Shunyu Liu
Email: [shunyu.liu.cs@gmail.com](mailto:)    Siyuan Liang
Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University
Email: [siyuan.liang@ntu.edu.sg](mailto:)    Chenyang Lyu
Affiliation: Alibaba Group
Email: [lyuchenyang.lcy@alibaba-inc.com](mailto:)    Dacheng Tao
^(†)^(†)thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Nanyang Technological

###### Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for empowering search
agents to tackle complex information-seeking tasks. However, since
acquiring external information necessitates web search, these agents are
highly susceptible to various adversarial attacks (e.g., malicious
information injection or stealthy context manipulation). Existing attack
strategies inevitably rely on static and human-crafted templates,
failing to emulate the dynamic and complex nature of real-world threats.
In this paper, we propose an adversarial self-evolution framework that
integrates bi-level optimization between the attacker’s strategy
evolution and the defender’s adaptive mitigation, to expose the
vulnerabilities of search agents. Specifically, we introduce the
Contrastive Rollout Evolutionary Optimization (CREO) method to drive the
directional evolution of the attack strategy population via contrastive
evolutionary signals. To provide a stable environment for this
continuous evolution, we further construct a controlled sandbox and
design fine-grained metrics to quantify internal vulnerabilities.
Extensive experiments across various multi-hop QA benchmarks and
frontier LLMs demonstrate that the proposed framework yields attack
efficacy superior to static baselines, underscoring the urgent need to
develop more robust defense frameworks.

### 1 Introduction

The paradigm of Large Language Models (LLMs) is rapidly shifting from
static knowledge bases toward highly autonomous search
agents \[[1](#bib.bib1), [2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3),
[4](#bib.bib4)\]. By deeply integrating web search and tool invocation,
these agents can perform complex multi-hop reasoning in real-world
scenarios \[[5](#bib.bib5), [6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7),
[8](#bib.bib50), [9](#bib.bib68), [10](#bib.bib51), [11](#bib.bib63)\].
However, this deep reliance on web search also exposes these agents to
RAG poisoning \[[12](#bib.bib8), [13](#bib.bib15), [14](#bib.bib16),
[15](#bib.bib27)\], a targeted attack that corrupts external knowledge
retrieval via malicious information injection. To evaluate this
vulnerability, testing environments have continuously evolved. Early
multi-hop QA benchmarks \[[16](#bib.bib9), [17](#bib.bib10),
[18](#bib.bib11)\] primarily relied on highly structured and homogeneous
corpora. In contrast, recent evaluations \[[19](#bib.bib12),
[20](#bib.bib13), [21](#bib.bib14)\] introduce cross-domain noise and
complex tool invocations. However, an inherent limitation of these
advanced evaluation environments is their static threat landscape. By
relying on manually predefined and rigidly injected noise, they struggle
to emulate the dynamic evolution of real-world adversarial information.
Consequently, static testing alone is insufficient to reveal these
underlying vulnerabilities, making it necessary to examine advanced
attack paradigms \[[22](#bib.bib49), [23](#bib.bib56)\].

However, existing attack paradigms suffer from fundamental structural
flaws across two dimensions: First, strategy generation is severely
bounded by human bias, as current mainstream attack
methods \[[12](#bib.bib8), [13](#bib.bib15), [14](#bib.bib16)\] rely
heavily on static, heuristic-based generation rules. Such rigid
templates not only constrain the exploration of the adversarial search
space but also yield attacks with poor stealthiness. For instance,
existing techniques often require injecting multiple malicious
documents \[[12](#bib.bib8), [24](#bib.bib17)\] to maintain attack
efficacy. This conspicuous pattern is easily filtered by an agent’s
multi-step verification process, preventing deep adversarial
penetration. Second, attack execution remains fundamentally
feedback-agnostic. Existing paradigms \[[12](#bib.bib8),
[13](#bib.bib15), [14](#bib.bib16)\] deploy predefined attack logics
that are entirely blind to the agent’s countermeasures. This blindness
ignores the continuous adaptation of real-world threats. Furthermore,
without a feedback mechanism, these static approaches quickly become
obsolete against upgraded defenses \[[25](#bib.bib18),
[26](#bib.bib19)\]. They therefore fail to probe the agent’s dynamic
defensive boundaries.

To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose framing the security
evaluation of search agents as a process of adversarial self-evolution,
formalized as a bi-level optimization problem. The inner loop models the
defender’s adaptive mitigation against the current attack pool, while
the outer loop drives the attacker’s continuous strategy evolution. To
efficiently solve the outer optimization, we introduce the Contrastive
Rollout Evolutionary Optimization (CREO) method as the core solver. CREO
completely eliminates the reliance on human-crafted templates. Operating
as a derivative-free evolutionary optimization solver within the
discrete natural language space, CREO leverages contrastive evolutionary
signals to drive the directional mutation, crossover, and selection of
the attack strategy population. By continuously evolving the attack
strategy pool, it exposes the vulnerabilities of search agents under
dynamic attacks. To ensure rigorous experimental control and internal
validity, we constructed a terabyte-scale controlled sandbox, enabling
the noise-free capture of reasoning pathways within a realistic,
high-noise environment. Finally, we introduce fine-grained cognitive
metrics. Utilizing adversarial success rate and adversarial paralysis
rate, they precisely quantify the depth to which the agent falls into
"logic hijacking" and "denial of service" when facing adversarial
induction. In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

- •
  We propose the first adversarial self-evolution framework for search
  agents, formalizing the adversarial interaction as a bi-level
  optimization problem. At its core, the CREO method employs contrastive
  evolutionary signals to drive the autonomous, directional mutation and
  selection of the attack strategy population. This mechanism breaks
  free from the reliance on human-crafted heuristics, enabling the
  continuous self-evolution of adversarial strategies.
- •
  We construct a controlled and rigorous evaluation system. A controlled
  sandbox is deployed to provide a stable, noise-free environment for
  the continuous evolution of attack strategies. Furthermore, we
  introduce fine-grained cognitive metrics that overcome traditional
  outcome-oriented limitations, precisely quantifying the internal
  vulnerabilities of reasoning agents.
- •
  Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks and frontier LLMs
  demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms existing
  static baselines. Notably, it achieves superior attack efficacy across
  various state-of-the-art LLMs, successfully exposing the deep
  vulnerabilities of search agents under dynamic and adaptive attacks.

### 2 Related Work

Search Agents. The paradigm of external knowledge acquisition has
shifted from passive retrieval \[[27](#bib.bib20)\] to autonomous
exploration driven by complex search agents \[[28](#bib.bib21)\]. By
equipping models with tool invocation capabilities \[[29](#bib.bib22),
[30](#bib.bib69)\] and coupling internal reasoning with external
actions \[[1](#bib.bib1), [2](#bib.bib2), [31](#bib.bib64),
[32](#bib.bib66), [33](#bib.bib67), [34](#bib.bib65)\], modern agents
can autonomously adjust multi-step strategies and perform complex
multi-hop reasoning in realistic, high-noise
environments \[[5](#bib.bib5), [6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7)\].
However, this highly automated information-gathering pipeline
significantly expands the system’s attack surface \[[8](#bib.bib50),
[10](#bib.bib51), [35](#bib.bib52), [36](#bib.bib53)\]. Operating
entirely without human intervention, agents processing unverified
external information are highly susceptible to stealthy document
poisoning, ultimately falling into irreversible logic hijacking.

RAG Poisoning. Existing poisoning attacks targeting the retrieval
pipeline \[[37](#bib.bib23)\] can be distinctly categorized into
white-box and black-box paradigms. White-box attacks delineate the
theoretical security boundaries of models from the feature dimension
through gradient optimization \[[38](#bib.bib24), [39](#bib.bib25),
[40](#bib.bib33)\] or neuron activation analysis \[[41](#bib.bib26)\].
However, due to the closed-source nature of commercial agents, this
strict access assumption regarding internal parameters makes them
inapplicable in real-world, dynamic external environments. Given these
limitations, we focus our research on practically feasible black-box
attacks \[[42](#bib.bib54), [43](#bib.bib55)\]. First, rule-based
tampering attacks \[[44](#bib.bib28)\] mechanically alter documents
using predefined static rules, such as entity substitution. Crucially,
this strategy is entirely decoupled from query semantics. Without
contextual optimization, the generated text is often rigid.
Consequently, these methods exhibit limited attack efficacy and are
easily blocked by routine filtering. Second, optimization-based
poisoning attacks \[[12](#bib.bib8), [13](#bib.bib15), [14](#bib.bib16),
[15](#bib.bib27), [24](#bib.bib17), [45](#bib.bib29), [46](#bib.bib30),
[47](#bib.bib31), [48](#bib.bib32)\], overcome these limitations by
deeply optimizing the injected text. These query-aware methods
proactively enhance retrievability and semantic deceptiveness. As a
result, they achieve significantly stronger penetration within the
retrieval pipeline. Third, evolutionary attacks \[[49](#bib.bib34),
[50](#bib.bib43), [23](#bib.bib56), [22](#bib.bib49)\] utilize model
feedback to drive continuous strategy self-evolution. Notably, this
dynamic paradigm remains largely unexplored in RAG poisoning. On the
defensive front, existing mechanisms operate across multiple
levels \[[51](#bib.bib57), [52](#bib.bib58), [53](#bib.bib59)\]. These
include statistical filtering \[[54](#bib.bib35), [55](#bib.bib36),
[56](#bib.bib37)\], retrieval aggregation \[[25](#bib.bib18),
[26](#bib.bib19)\], and generation-level denoising \[[57](#bib.bib38),
[58](#bib.bib39), [59](#bib.bib40)\]. Despite these advancements,
current attack and defense schemes remain fundamentally static. They
lack a genuine mechanism for dynamic adversarial interaction.

### 3 Methodology

This section details the proposed adversarial self-evolution evaluation
framework
(Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents")).
We sequentially present its bi-level optimization formalization
(Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Overall Framework: Adversarial Self-Evolution via Bi-level Optimization ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents")),
the CREO solver grounded in evolutionary optimization
(Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Contrastive Rollout Evolutionary Optimization (CREO) ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents")),
and the controlled evaluation environment
(Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Controlled Evaluation Environment ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents")).

![Refer to caption](2611.03754v1/figure1.png)

#### 3.1 Overall Framework: Adversarial Self-Evolution via Bi-level Optimization

We formalize the security evaluation of search agents as a process of
adversarial self-evolution, modeled as a bi-level optimization problem
over a discrete natural language space. To efficiently solve this
problem, we model the interaction between the attacker and the defender
as two mutually coupled optimization processes. The outer loop drives
the attacker’s continuous strategy evolution, while the inner loop
models the defender’s adaptive mitigation. Specifically, we model the
attacker’s outer optimization as an evolutionary optimization
problem \[[60](#bib.bib41), [61](#bib.bib42), [50](#bib.bib43)\], with
the strategy pool serving as the population. Each individual contains a
natural-language mechanism for constructing adversarial documents, and
its fitness is measured by its empirical attack success rate on a fixed
evaluation set. CREO uses contrastive rollout feedback to guide mutation
and crossover, and updates the population through fitness-based
selection and diversity maintenance to reliably find effective attack
strategies. Given a multi-hop question-answering task domain
$`\mathcal{D}`$, let $`\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{K}}`$ denote the defending
agent equipped with defensive knowledge $`\mathcal{K}`$, where
$`\mathcal{K}_{t}`$ denotes the knowledge state at round $`t`$, and
$`\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{P}}`$ denote the attacking agent operating with
strategy pool $`\mathcal{P}`$, where $`\mathcal{P}_{t}`$ denotes the
strategy pool at round $`t`$.

1. Inner Loop: Defender’s Adaptive Mitigation

In each round, the defending agent aims to maximize its accuracy on the
task domain against the attacker’s current strategy pool
$`\mathcal{P}_{t-1}`$. Formally, the inner optimization objective is
defined as:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{K}_{t}^{*}=\arg\max_{\mathcal{K}}\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}}[\text{Acc}(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{K}}(q,\ \mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{P}_{t-1}}(q)))],
``` |  | (1) |

where $`q`$ is a question sampled from task domain $`\mathcal{D}`$,
$`\mathcal{P}_{t-1}`$ is the attacker’s strategy pool inherited from the
previous adversarial evolution round, and $`\text{Acc}(\cdot)`$ measures
the defending agent’s question-answering accuracy under adversarial
attack conditions.

Equation (1) defines an ideal optimization objective over
natural-language defensive knowledge $`\mathcal{K}`$. Under black-box
constraints, model parameters are inaccessible, while exhaustive search
or direct gradient-based optimization over natural-language knowledge is
impractical. We therefore adopt an approximate implementation based on
strategy disclosure. Specifically, we transcribe the attack mechanisms
and vulnerable question types in the previous round’s exposed strategy
pool $`\mathcal{P}_{t-1}`$ into structured descriptions of known attack
patterns and inject them into the defender’s system prompt as defensive
knowledge $`\mathcal{K}_{t}`$. Defensive knowledge is thus derived from
the exposed strategy pool and updated accordingly. By providing the
defender with full information about the exposed strategy pool, this
protocol establishes a well-informed defense condition for a stringent
adversarial stress test of search agents. The defense comparisons in
Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents")
provide a basis for adopting this evaluation setting.

2. Outer Loop: Attacker’s Strategy Evolution

Facing the upgraded agent $`\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{K}_{t}}`$, the
attacker must evolve a new strategy pool $`\mathcal{P}_{t}`$ from the
original strategies to maximize the probability of disrupting the
agent’s decision-making chain. By introducing a cognitive state
evaluation function $`J(\cdot)`$, which audits the agent’s full
reasoning chain and outputs a cognitive state label from
$`\{\text{DA, CP, Refuted, Neutral}\}`$, the outer attack optimization
objective is formalized as seeking the optimal strategy pool
$`\mathcal{P}_{t}^{*}`$ that maximizes the probability of driving the
agent into one of two compromised cognitive states across the task
domain:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{P}_{t}^{*}=\arg\max_{\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}}[\mathbb{I}(J(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{K}_{t}}(q,\ \mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{P}}(q)))\in\{\text{DA},\text{CP}\})],
``` |  | (2) |

where $`\mathbb{I}(\cdot)`$ is the indicator function,
$`\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{P}}(q)`$ denotes the attacking agent generating
adversarial documents from strategy pool $`\mathcal{P}`$ and injecting
them into the retrieval list, DA (Direct Adoption) and CP (Cognitive
Paralysis) are two cognitive states indicating the agent has been
successfully compromised. We use CREO to approximate this outer
optimization objective through population-based iteration. In Round 0,
we perform multiple rollouts for each selected training question under a
generic document-forgery instruction. An LLM then contrasts the
resulting interaction traces to extract and consolidate natural-language
attack strategies into the initial pool $`\mathcal{P}_{0}`$. Subsequent
rounds update the strategy pool $`\mathcal{P}_{t}`$ through continued
strategy evolution and selection. During attack execution, the attacking
agent selects an applicable strategy from the pool based on the current
question, generates a forged document, and injects it into the retrieval
results, which are then reranked using the same retrieval rules. Details
of initialization, strategy formats, and attack execution are provided
in Appendix B.

#### 3.2 Contrastive Rollout Evolutionary Optimization (CREO)

As the core solver for the outer attack optimization, CREO models the
attack strategy pool as an evolutionary population driven by contrastive
evolution signals. It generates child strategies via directional
mutation and integrates multi-source evolution signals through crossover
recombination, while homogeneity constraints maintain population
diversity. Through iterative population evolution, CREO continuously
refines the attack strategy pool across multiple rounds.

##### 3.2.1 Formal Definition of Attack Strategy

We formalize each adversarial strategy as a triplet
$`s=(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G},\mathcal{C}_{\phi})`$:

Deception Mechanism ($`\mathcal{M}`$): The core executable component of
the strategy, describing in natural language the logic for constructing
forged documents to mislead the agent’s reasoning process.

Empirical Generalization Advantage ($`\mathcal{G}`$): The individual
fitness of the strategy, measuring its empirical attack success rate on
a fixed evaluation set $`\mathcal{D}_{eval}\subset\mathcal{D}`$.
Strategies with zero fitness are immediately pruned from the population,
ensuring all individuals maintain an attack advantage.

Dynamic Contextual Profile ($`\mathcal{C}_{\phi}`$): A structured
characterization of the question types where strategy $`\mathcal{M}`$
succeeds or fails, extracted by an LLM from the success set
$`\mathcal{D}_{succ}`$ and failure set $`\mathcal{D}_{fail}`$ produced
during the strategy evaluation process:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{C}_{\phi}=\text{LLM}_{profile}({\text{DeEntify}(q)\mid q\in\mathcal{D}_{succ}},{\text{DeEntify}(q)\mid q\in\mathcal{D}_{fail}}),
``` |  | (3) |

where $`\mathcal{D}_{succ}`$ and $`\mathcal{D}_{fail}`$ are the sets of
questions on which $`\mathcal{M}`$ succeeds and fails respectively,
$`\text{LLM}_{profile}(\cdot)`$ denotes an LLM that summarizes the
operational boundaries of the strategy, and $`\text{DeEntify}(\cdot)`$
replaces named entities in the queries with abstract placeholders (e.g.,
\[PERSON_1\]), preventing $`\mathcal{C}_{\phi}`$ from overfitting to
specific entities.

##### 3.2.2 Population Evolution via Contrastive Rollout

CREO drives the continuous evolution of the attack strategy population
via a two-stage contrastive rollout mechanism, distinguishing between a
population initialization stage (Round 0) and a continuous evolution
stage (Round $`t\geq 1`$). Within each round, contrastive evolution
signals are first extracted from the agent’s behavioral traces, then
used to drive directional mutation and crossover recombination, followed
by selection and diversity maintenance.

Round 0: Population Initialization. Without relying on any human-crafted
priors, the system executes $`K`$ independent parallel reasoning passes
on the same set of queries. For each query $`q`$, the system then
collects $`K`$ reasoning traces:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{T}_{0}(q)=\{\tau_{1}(q),\tau_{2}(q),\dots,\tau_{K}(q)\},
``` |  | (4) |

where $`\tau_{k}(q)`$ denotes the $`k`$-th reasoning trace on query
$`q`$, and $`K`$ is the number of parallel passes. By comparing
behavioral differences across these traces, the system extracts initial
attack logic with a relative advantage as seed individuals, forming the
initial population $`\mathcal{P}_{0}`$.

Round $`t\geq 1`$: Continuous Evolution. The parent strategy
$`s_{parent}=(\mathcal{M}_{parent},\mathcal{G}_{parent},\mathcal{C}_{\phi_{parent}})`$
is applied to diverse queries, and the agent’s full behavioral traces
are captured and labeled with success or failure outcomes, forming the
contrastive evolution signals:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{S}_{contrast}=\{\tau^{+}\mid\tau^{+}\in\mathcal{T}_{succ}\}\cup\{\tau^{-}\mid\tau^{-}\in\mathcal{T}_{fail}\},
``` |  | (5) |

where $`\tau^{+}`$ and $`\tau^{-}`$ denote success and failure traces
respectively, and $`\mathcal{T}_{succ}`$ and $`\mathcal{T}_{fail}`$ are
the corresponding sets of behavioral traces collected during evaluation.

Directional Mutation and Crossover Recombination. The parent mechanism
$`\mathcal{M}_{parent}`$, its profile $`\mathcal{C}_{\phi_{parent}}`$,
and the contrastive evolution signals $`\mathcal{S}_{contrast}`$ are
jointly fed into the evolutionary operator. Since traces from diverse
query scenarios carry complementary information, their fusion
constitutes the crossover recombination operation, providing directional
guidance for mutation. The evolutionary operator then performs
directional mutation on the parent mechanism, generating a child
mechanism
$`\mathcal{M}_{child}=\text{Mutate}(\mathcal{M}_{parent},\mathcal{C}_{\phi_{parent}},\mathcal{S}_{contrast})`$,
whose fitness is evaluated as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{G}(s)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{eval}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{D}_{eval}}\mathbb{I}(J(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{K}}(q,\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{P}}(q)))\in\{\text{DA},\text{CP}\}).
``` |  | (6) |

Selection and Diversity Maintenance. The child strategy
$`s_{child}=(\mathcal{M}_{child},\mathcal{G}_{child},\mathcal{C}_{\phi_{child}})`$
is evaluated against all existing strategies by an LLM to judge whether
it covers the same question scenarios. If highly homogeneous, the child
replaces the parent only when
$`\mathcal{G}_{child}>\mathcal{G}_{parent}`$, enforcing selection
pressure. If heterogeneous and the population has reached capacity, it
replaces the individual with the lowest historical fitness, maintaining
population diversity. A formal monotonicity property of this selection
mechanism is provided in
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Theoretical Property of CREO ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents").

#### 3.3 Controlled Evaluation Environment

To support adversarial evolution, we extend the DeepResearchGym
framework \[[62](#bib.bib44)\] to construct a dedicated controlled
sandbox. At the physical layer, system-level stochasticity is eliminated
by fixing retrieval parameters and enforcing strict sorting rules. At
the observation layer, a Dynamic Retrieval Interceptor enables stealthy
hot-injection of adversarial text into the retrieval list without
polluting the original knowledge base. At the cognitive layer, an
LLM-as-a-Judge audits the agent’s complete reasoning chain at each
adversarial round to precisely capture its internal cognitive state.
Architectural details are provided in the
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Controlled Sandbox Architecture ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents").

For evaluation metrics, we redefine existing metrics and introduce a
novel one. Rigorous Adversarial Accuracy (Acc) requires the agent to
produce a correct answer while its reasoning process remains entirely
free from adversarial interference. Adversarial Success Rate (ASR)
operates at the reasoning-trace level, judging an attack successful only
when the agent explicitly incorporates forged documents as valid
evidence, which is stricter than conventional ASR. Adversarial Paralysis
Rate (APR) is a novel metric introduced for complex reasoning agents,
triggered when adversarial text creates irreconcilable contradictions
with authentic documents, causing the agent to refuse to answer. Formal
definitions of all metrics are provided in the
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Formal Definitions of Evaluation Metrics ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents").

Summary. Within the adversarial self-evolution framework, the attacker
and defender engage in continuous co-evolution through bi-level
optimization: the defender adaptively updates its defensive knowledge,
while CREO drives the outer optimization through contrastive
signal-guided directional mutation and crossover recombination,
maintaining population diversity via homogeneity constraints. Across
multiple rounds, this process continuously refines the attack strategy
pool under dynamic defensive pressure. The controlled sandbox provides a
stable experimental foundation, while fine-grained cognitive metrics
precisely quantify the agent’s internal reasoning vulnerabilities.

### 4 Experiment

#### 4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets and Target Agents. We evaluate our framework on three multi-hop
QA benchmarks: HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue, sampling 100
training and 100 test queries per dataset. Only questions and
ground-truth answers are retained; all retrieval operates exclusively
within our sandbox. We deploy five target LLMs spanning diverse
capability tiers as target search agents:
Qwen-Turbo \[[63](#bib.bib45)\], Qwen3-Max \[[63](#bib.bib45)\],
DeepSeek-V3.2 \[[64](#bib.bib46)\], Kimi-K2.5 \[[65](#bib.bib47)\], and
GLM-5.1 \[[66](#bib.bib48)\].

Baselines and Metrics. We benchmark CREO against two representative
paradigms drawn from distinct generation strategies. Rule-based
Tampering (FactSwap) substitutes critical answer entities in retrieved
authentic documents with type-consistent counterparts.
Optimization-based Poisoning (AuthChain) is a query-aware attack that
jointly optimizes injected text for retrievability and semantic
deceptiveness. Performance is evaluated via Rigorous Adversarial
Accuracy ($`Acc`$), Adversarial Success Rate ($`ASR`$), and Adversarial
Paralysis Rate ($`APR`$).

Adversarial Evolution Settings. Evaluations are conducted under two
complementary conditions within the same iterative process: Evo
(Evolutionary Advantage Setting), where the attack strategy pool evolves
against the previous round’s static defense; and Sync (Synchronous
Setting), where defense mechanisms update synchronously with the current
attack pool.

Implementation Details. The framework runs a contrastive initialization
(Round 0) followed by three evolution rounds (Rounds 1–3), with strategy
pool capacity capped at 10 individuals. Further configurations are
detailed in the
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents").

Overall Superiority over Baselines. As shown in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents"),
CREO demonstrates consistent and substantial attack superiority over
both static baselines. Even at Round 1, CREO achieves substantially
lower Acc than both static baselines on most (model, dataset)
combinations, while inducing both DA and CP dimensions of cognitive
compromise. Taking GLM-5.1 on MuSiQue as a representative example, Acc
drops from 82 (Base) to 41 under AuthChain, while CREO further reduces
it to 16 within a single evolutionary round. CREO maintains attack
efficacy even under the Sync condition, where defenses update
synchronously with the attack pool, achieving lower Acc than baselines
in most (model, dataset) combinations at Round 1. Complete per-model and
per-dataset visualizations across all evolution rounds are provided in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Visualization of Main Results ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents").

Cognitive Paralysis as a Distinct Attack Dimension. As shown in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents"),
both FactSwap and AuthChain yield substantially lower APR than CREO
across all settings, with CREO’s evolved strategies pushing APR well
above baseline levels across most models and datasets by Round 3. This
contrast reveals a fundamental limitation of static paradigms: their
forged documents fail to construct genuine contradictions against
authentic retrieval results. Unlike ASR, where the agent is directly
deceived into adopting forged evidence, APR reflects a less severe but
non-trivial outcome where the agent detects a conflict and cannot
resolve it. That CREO simultaneously drives both dimensions confirms the
breadth of its evolved strategies across the vulnerability spectrum.

Table 2: APR results highlighting the cognitive paralysis dimension
induced by CREO’s evolved strategies across three rounds.

Evolution Across Rounds. In the main experiments, attack strategies and
defensive knowledge evolve together, so changes in metrics across rounds
reflect updates on both sides. Defensive knowledge is empty in Round 1
under Evo, while subsequent Evo rounds use the previous round’s
defensive knowledge, and Sync updates the defense based on the current
attack strategy pool. Results across rounds should therefore be
interpreted in the context of their corresponding defense conditions.

To capture both direct adoption and cognitive paralysis, we use the
total attack success rate, $`\mathrm{TASR}=\mathrm{ASR}+\mathrm{APR}`$,
averaged over 15 model–dataset combinations. Across the three rounds,
CREO achieves mean Evo TASRs of 64.2–74.6% and mean Sync TASRs of
60.5–64.9% following synchronized defense updates. In comparison, the
mean Evo/Sync TASRs are 20.9%/18.1% for FactSwap and 55.7%/37.5% for
AuthChain. CREO’s mean Sync TASR remains higher than the mean Evo TASR
of each static baseline. Furthermore, across the two round transitions,
mean TASR recovers by 2.4 and 4.7 percentage points, respectively, from
the previous round’s Sync phase to the next round’s Evo phase. These
results provide evidence that attack strategies can adapt to updated
defenses through evolution.

To further assess the effectiveness of attack-strategy evolution, we
held defensive knowledge derived from the Round 0 strategy pool fixed
and allowed only the attack strategies to evolve, as reported in
Appendix [E.4](#A5.SS4 "E.4 Validation of Cross-Round Evolution ‣ Appendix E Supplementary Experiments ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents").
In the evaluated settings, Round 3 yields lower Acc than Round 1.
Re-evaluation without defense and cross-round attacker–defender transfer
experiments also show that later-round strategies remain effective under
other defense conditions. These results provide additional evidence for
CREO’s cross-round strategy evolution and its transfer across the tested
defense conditions.

Generalization Across Datasets and Models. CREO achieves consistent
attack efficacy across all three datasets, validating the framework’s
generalization across diverse question structures and reasoning
configurations. Furthermore, target models across all capability tiers
remain vulnerable, confirming that the framework’s effectiveness is
independent of specific model architectures.

#### 4.3 Ablation Study

Ablation on Population Evolution Mechanism. To validate the
effectiveness of population iteration and directed mutation-crossover,
we design two ablation variants against the full method. Static Pool
removes the population iteration component entirely, freezing the
strategy pool after Round 0 initialization. Random Evolution retains
population iteration but removes the contrastive evolution signal,
degenerating directed mutation and crossover into blind random mutation.
All three variants share an identical Round 0 initial population, with
Round 1 as the comparison window where defensive knowledge is empty
across all groups, ensuring clean variable control.

| Variant | Evo.           | Dir.           | Qwen-T     | Qwen3-M    | Kimi    | GLM     |
|---------|----------------|----------------|------------|------------|---------|---------|
|         |                |                | (HotpotQA) | (HotpotQA) | (2Wiki) | (2Wiki) |
| Static  | $`\times`$     | $`\times`$     | 38%        | 23%        | 31%     | 22%     |
| Random  | $`\checkmark`$ | $`\times`$     | 34%        | 24%        | 36%     | 20%     |
| Full    | $`\checkmark`$ | $`\checkmark`$ | 28%        | 20%        | 28%     | 16%     |

Table 3: Ablation Study (Round 1). We report True Accuracy (Acc
$`\downarrow`$). Lower indicates stronger attack. Evo.: Evolution
Action; Dir.: Directed Feedback.

As shown in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents"),
Static Pool and Random Evolution show comparable performance, while Full
CREO achieves the lowest Acc across all models. Random Evolution does
not consistently outperform Static Pool—improving on some models while
underperforming on others—demonstrating that population iteration
without directed contrastive signals fails to yield reliable gains. Full
CREO achieves the lowest Acc across all models, validating that the
contrastive evolution signal providing directed mutation is the core
mechanism driving effective strategy population evolution.

Ablation on Diversity Maintenance Mechanism. To validate the necessity
of the homogeneity constraint, we compare Full CREO against a
No-Constraint variant. In Full CREO, heterogeneous child strategies
replace the lowest-fitness individual in the pool, while homogeneous
children enter only upon strictly outperforming their parent;
No-Constraint removes this gate, degenerating population selection into
greedy evolution without diversity control.

As shown in
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents"),
No-Constraint yields a mean pairwise strategy similarity of 0.583 versus
0.270 for Full CREO, confirming that greedy evolution rapidly drives the
strategy pool toward homogeneous convergence, with multiple strategies
redundantly targeting the same question subset. This validates that the
homogeneity constraint’s core value lies in maintaining population-level
coverage diversity rather than optimizing individual strategy fitness.

![Refer to caption](2611.03754v1/ablation_nc.png)

(b) No-Constraint (Greedy)

#### 4.4 Analysis

Defense Necessity Analysis. As shown in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents"),
Keyword Filter and Perplexity Filter provide negligible protection
against CREO’s evolved attacks, with total interference rates remaining
comparable to the No Defense baseline. This is attributable to the
semantic fluency and contextual coherence of evolved forged documents,
which naturally evade pattern-matching and perplexity-based anomaly
detection. RobustRAG achieves moderate suppression through its
isolate-and-aggregate strategy, yet fails to fundamentally block
adversarial penetration. Only CREO Defense yields substantial
interference reduction (Qwen-Turbo: 53%, GLM-5.1: 17%),

Figure 3: Total interference rate under different defense modes
(HotpotQA, 100 queries).

confirming that evolved attack strategies construct adversarial patterns
beyond the recognition boundary of existing static defenses. This
justifies CREO’s use of strategy-aware defense as a stringent evaluation
setting: maintaining significant attack efficacy under a defense with
maximal information about the attack pool constitutes a rigorous stress
test of search agent security boundaries.

Strategy Pool Diversity Analysis. After three rounds of evolution,
CREO’s strategy pool exhibits a highly heterogeneous distribution of
attack patterns, spanning from identity obfuscation and multi-source
contradiction construction to multi-hop reasoning poisoning, with more
sophisticated patterns emerging exclusively in later rounds. This
validates that the homogeneity constraint effectively maintains
population diversity under sustained evolutionary pressure, enabling
different strategies to target distinct question topologies in a
complementary manner. A complete snapshot of the strategy pool and
detailed coverage analysis are provided in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Strategy Pool Evolution Analysis ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents").

#### 4.5 Case Study

Case 1: Strategy Evolution

The Round 0 parent strategy lacks concrete operational constraints,
making its coarse-grained interference easily bypassed by multi-step
verification:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Driven by contrastive evolution signals, CREO performs directional
mutation on the parent mechanism to generate the child strategy:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The child strategy upgrades from vague contradiction construction to
multi-dimensional forging guidelines, elevating the attack objective
from simple interference to directly triggering logic hijacking via a
consensus illusion. This evolutionary trajectory demonstrates that CREO
can achieve substantial strategy advancement through iteration,
continuously evolving more stealthy and destructive attack strategies to
breach agent defenses.

Case 2: Question-level Attack-Defense Evolution

As shown in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.5 Case Study ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents"),
Round 1 attack initially succeeds but is suppressed once defense
knowledge is updated. Round 2 defenses successfully identify the attack
pattern under both Evo and Sync conditions. In Round 3, CREO shifts to
micro-mutation: retaining real data as a trust anchor while redirecting
tampering toward a less salient variable. Even as the agent explicitly
recognizes the attack pattern, logical penetration is achieved,
demonstrating the adaptive capacity of evolved strategies under
sustained defensive pressure.

![Refer to caption](2611.03754v1/case_study.png)

Figure 4: Round-by-round attack-defense trajectory on a representative
query. Each round shows the evolved attack strategy alongside the
agent’s reasoning outcome under the Evo and Sync conditions,
respectively, illustrating how the two settings diverge over successive
rounds.

### 5 Conclusion

We propose CREO, the first adversarial self-evolution framework for
search agents. CREO formalizes the attacker-defender interaction as a
bi-level optimization problem, employing contrastive rollout
evolutionary optimization to drive directional strategy population
evolution while maintaining population diversity via homogeneity
constraints, overcoming the fundamental limitation of static attack
paradigms that lack dynamic adaptability. The constructed controlled
sandbox provides a standardized environment for adversarial security
evaluation, while fine-grained cognitive metrics overcome the
limitations of traditional outcome-oriented assessment. Extensive
experiments across diverse benchmarks and target models demonstrate
consistent attack superiority over static baselines, with significant
attack efficacy maintained even under synchronous defense updates.

Limitations and Future Work. The current framework validates adversarial
self-evolution under multi-hop QA settings. However, multi-hop QA
involves relatively fixed retrieval structures, whereas long-chain
reasoning agents such as Deep Research require more complex tool
invocations and dynamic information aggregation. The framework’s
generalizability to such settings remains an open question. Future work
will therefore focus on extending the framework to more complex
autonomous search scenarios to broaden the security evaluation
landscape. Developing adaptive defense mechanisms capable of countering
evolutionary attacks will further establish more robust security
boundaries for next-generation search agents in dynamic adversarial
environments.

## Appendix

### Table of Contents

### Appendix A Visualization of Main Results

Figures [5](#A1.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Appendix A Visualization of Main Results ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents")
and [6](#A1.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix A Visualization of Main Results ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents")
present Acc and ASR across all adversarial evolution rounds under both
Evo and Sync conditions, covering five target models on three
benchmarks. Horizontal dashed lines indicate the static baselines
(FactSwap and AuthChain), and the dotted line denotes unattacked base
accuracy. CREO achieves lower Acc and higher ASR than both static
baselines on most (model, dataset) combinations as early as Round 1, and
sustains attack efficacy even under Sync, where defenses update
synchronously with the evolving attack
pool.Figure [6](#A1.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix A Visualization of Main Results ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents")
further reports APR across all settings. The stark contrast between the
near-zero APR of static baselines and the substantially elevated APR
induced by CREO confirms that cognitive paralysis is a distinct attack
dimension static poisoning fundamentally fails to trigger, with certain
combinations (e.g., DeepSeek-V3.2) exceeding APR 75 by Round 3.

Figure 5: Acc and ASR across adversarial evolution rounds (Part I):
HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA, shown for both Evo and Sync conditions.

Figure 6: Acc and ASR across adversarial evolution rounds (Part II):
MuSiQue. APR comparison across all datasets and target models under CREO
vs. static baselines.

### Appendix B Implementation Details

###### Evolution Configuration.

The framework executes a contrastive initialization phase (Round 0)
followed by three adversarial evolution rounds (Rounds 1–3). During
Round 0, $`K{=}3`$ parallel rollout passes are performed per query over
a set of 20 training questions to extract seed individuals for the
initial strategy population. Each subsequent evolution round samples 3
queries per parent strategy for child generation. The strategy pool
capacity is capped at $`N{=}10`$ individuals throughout all rounds. The
fixed evaluation set $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{eval}}`$ consists of the first
20 questions from the training split, held constant across all rounds to
ensure a consistent fitness signal. All experiments use a global random
seed of 42 for reproducibility.

###### Dataset and Target Models.

Experiments are conducted on three multi-hop QA benchmarks: HotpotQA,
2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue. For each dataset, 100 questions are
sampled for training and 100 for testing. Five frontier LLMs are
evaluated as target search agents: Qwen-Turbo, Qwen3-Max, DeepSeek-V3.2,
Kimi-K2.5, and GLM-5.1, accessed via Alibaba Cloud’s DashScope API.
Chain-of-thought thinking mode is disabled for all models to ensure
deterministic and comparable reasoning traces.

###### Retrieval and Encoding.

The retrieval service is deployed locally via a DiskANN-based index over
the FineWeb corpus. Query encoding is performed using
MiniCPM-Embedding-Light, with a task-specific instruction prefix
prepended to each query. Named entity de-identification (DeEntify) is
implemented via spaCy, replacing recognized entities with abstract
type-consistent placeholders (e.g., \[PERSON_1\]); results are cached to
avoid redundant processing across rounds.

###### Infrastructure.

All experiments are conducted on an Alibaba Cloud server. Parallel tool
calls are disabled to preserve strict sequential reasoning trace capture
within the controlled sandbox.

###### Notation and Data Formats.

Each strategy individual is represented as
$`s=(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G},\mathcal{C}_{\phi})`$, and parent and child
strategies share this structure. Here, $`\mathcal{M}`$ is a
natural-language attack mechanism, $`\mathcal{G}`$ is its empirical
fitness on the fixed evaluation set, and $`\mathcal{C}_{\phi}`$ is a
structured profile of its operational scope. The profile contains three
fields, strength, weakness, and reasoning, each storing natural-language
text. The ordinary letter $`K`$ denotes the number of initialization
rollouts, whereas $`\mathcal{K}`$ denotes defensive knowledge.
Tables [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Notation and Data Formats. ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents")
and [5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Notation and Data Formats. ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents")
summarize the variables and the input/output representations of the
framework’s functions.

[TABLE]

Table 4: Variables and data representations used in the framework.

|  Function or Operation |  Input |  Output and Format |
|----|----|----|
|  $`\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{P}}(q)`$ |  Question and strategy-pool context; document generation also uses the reference answer. |  Generated adversarial documents and their retrieval injection. The generation template returns JSON with text, url, and title. |
|  $`\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{K}}(\cdot)`$ |  Question, retrieval results, and defensive-knowledge context. |  The agent’s interaction trace and final answer. |
|  $`J(\cdot)`$ |  Complete interaction trace, with the question, ground truth, and forged document as context. |  A cognitive-state label in $`\{\mathrm{DA},\mathrm{CP},\mathrm{Refuted},\mathrm{Neutral}\}`$. |
|  $`\mathrm{Acc}(\cdot)`$ |  Answer correctness and cognitive state. |  A binary indicator of a correct answer without DA or CP; dataset accuracy is its mean. |
|  $`\mathbb{I}(\cdot)`$ |  A Boolean condition. |  $`1`$ if the condition holds, and $`0`$ otherwise. |
|  $`\mathcal{G}(s)`$ |  Attack outcomes for strategy $`s`$ on the fixed evaluation set. |  The empirical proportion of DA or CP outcomes, in $`[0,1]`$. |
|  $`\mathrm{DeEntify}(\cdot)`$ |  Question text. |  Text with named entities replaced by type-consistent placeholders. |
|  $`\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{profile}}(\cdot)`$ |  De-identified successful and failed question sets. |  The profile $`\mathcal{C}_{\phi}`$, in the three-field JSON format described above. |
|  $`\mathrm{Mutate}(\cdot)`$ |  Parent mechanism, parent profile, and contrastive evolution signals. |  The child mechanism $`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{child}}`$, read from the generated child_strategy field. |
|  LLM homogeneity judge |  Child mechanism and profile, together with the existing strategy pool. |  JSON containing is_duplicate, most_similar_idx, and similarity_reasoning. |

Table 5: Inputs, outputs, and data formats of the framework’s functions.

The starred quantities $`\mathcal{K}_{t}^{*}`$ and
$`\mathcal{P}_{t}^{*}`$ denote solutions to the ideal optimization
objectives. In the experiments, $`\mathcal{K}_{t}`$ and
$`\mathcal{P}_{t}`$ are constructed through defensive-knowledge
transcription and strategy-population iteration, respectively.

###### Strategy Generation and Execution.

During Round 0, we use a generic instruction to generate forged
documents containing incorrect answers and perform multiple rollouts for
the same training question, recording attack outcomes and complete
interaction traces. When all attempts fail, an LLM analyzes the failure
traces to identify why the attacks were detected or ineffective and
proposes an abstract attack mechanism. When outcomes differ, it extracts
reusable attack principles from successful cases. The extracted
strategies are consolidated, merged, and deduplicated, then evaluated on
the fixed evaluation set. Zero-fitness candidates are discarded to form
the initial pool $`\mathcal{P}_{0}`$. Parent mechanisms in the first
evolution round originate from these retained seeds, while later rounds
select parents from the current pool. The extraction and compression
prompts are provided in Appendix C.5.

During subsequent evolution, questions are sampled for each parent
strategy and attacks are executed. The judge $`J(\cdot)`$ audits the
resulting traces, treating DA or CP as attack success and the remaining
states as failure. The parent mechanism, contextual profile, and
contrastive signals jointly enter the LLM evolutionary operator to
generate a child mechanism. Fusion of complementary interaction signals
from different query scenarios constitutes crossover and guides
directional mutation. The child is then evaluated on the fixed
evaluation set to obtain its fitness and profile before homogeneity
assessment and selection. A homogeneous child replaces its parent only
when its fitness is higher. A heterogeneous child is added when capacity
remains; otherwise, it replaces the individual with the lowest
historical fitness. Homogeneity assessment considers both the core
deception mechanism and effective target question types. The evolution,
profile-extraction, and homogeneity-assessment prompts are provided in
Appendices C.3, C.4, and C.6, respectively.

During attack execution, the attacking agent selects an applicable
strategy for the current question and supplies the question, reference
answer, and strategy mechanism to the document-generation prompt. The
generated forged document contains an incorrect answer and is
represented as JSON with text, url, and title; the template is provided
in Appendix C.7. The Dynamic Retrieval Interceptor merges the forged
document with authentic retrieval results, re-sorts the combined list by
ascending L2 distance, and returns the top-$`k`$ entries to the agent.
Injection is performed through query-level in-memory interception.
Details of retrieval and injection are provided in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Controlled Sandbox Architecture ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents").

Defensive knowledge is constructed from the strategy pool disclosed
under the corresponding evaluation condition. Attack mechanisms and
vulnerable question types are transcribed into known attack patterns and
inserted into the system context using the informed-defense addon in
Appendix C.1. In the main experiments, Round 1 Evo uses empty defensive
knowledge, subsequent Evo rounds retain the previous round’s defensive
knowledge, and Sync updates that knowledge based on the current round’s
strategy pool. Defensive knowledge therefore changes with strategy
disclosure and evaluation phase, implementing adaptation through
knowledge supplied in the system prompt.

### Appendix D Strategy Pool Evolution Analysis

This appendix provides a complete snapshot of CREO’s final strategy pool
after three rounds of evolution, along with a detailed analysis of
representative evolutionary trajectories. Together, these materials
substantiate the claim that CREO’s evolutionary mechanism successfully
maintains a heterogeneous attack population while continuously refining
individual strategies toward greater stealth and effectiveness.

#### Final Strategy Pool Snapshot

After three rounds of evolution, the strategy pool contains the
following ten attack strategies:

- •
  Identity Obfuscation (Round 0): Presents two mutually contradictory
  claims about a subject’s primary professional identity with equal
  credibility, forcing the agent into an irresolvable ambiguity that
  prevents a definitive answer. Targets single-hop factual queries.
- •
  Multi-source Contradiction (Round 0): Simultaneously injects documents
  containing plausible false information alongside documents with
  correct information, preventing the agent from establishing an
  authoritative answer. Targets direct comparison and ordering queries.
- •
  Temporal Confusion (Round 0): Constructs mutually contradictory
  historical narratives within retrieved documents to disrupt temporal
  context, blocking the agent’s fact verification across time-dependent
  information. Targets compound entity description queries.
- •
  False Categorical Linking (Round 0): Injects documents establishing
  fabricated categorical relationships between entities, paired with
  authentic-looking documents that omit or contradict the link,
  exploiting the agent’s conflict resolution mechanism. Targets entity
  attribute substitution queries.
- •
  False Fact Chain (Round 1): Fabricates a series of interconnected
  documents that collectively construct a multi-step false knowledge
  network, making the incorrect answer appear to have complete logical
  derivation support. Targets shared attribute identification queries.
- •
  Semantic Entrapment (Round 1): A primary document establishes a clear
  factual claim while auxiliary documents subtly redefine the scope or
  applicability of key terms, creating definitional conflicts that
  corrupt the agent’s logical lookup process. Targets single-entity
  attribute queries.
- •
  Authority Document Noise Injection (Round 2): Generates a document
  that correctly answers the core question while embedding subtle
  contradictions in secondary attributes, exploiting the agent’s
  tendency to reconcile internal inconsistencies toward an incorrect
  conclusion. Targets binary comparative queries.
- •
  Multi-hop Reasoning Poisoning (Round 3): Inserts a fabricated
  intermediate entity between two target entities, redirecting the
  agent’s chain-of-thought reasoning through a false bridge node to
  produce an incorrect final answer. Targets multi-hop reasoning
  queries.
- •
  Dual-document Entity Confusion (Round 3): Generates a primary document
  misattributing real events or properties to a similar entity,
  reinforced by a secondary document corroborating the same false
  attribution from a different perspective, inducing the agent to
  conflate distinct entities. Targets simple comparative queries.
- •
  Single-document Authority Deception (Round 3): Generates a single
  document mimicking the format of an official registry or database
  entry that pre-establishes a false key connection between two
  entities, short-circuiting the agent’s cross-document reasoning with a
  single “authoritative” source. Targets comparative and relational
  judgment queries.

The pool covers six distinct attack dimensions—temporal disruption,
entity confusion, semantic manipulation, multi-hop reasoning corruption,
authority exploitation, and contradiction induction—confirming that
CREO’s homogeneity constraint successfully prevents population collapse
toward a single dominant attack pattern. Four strategies originate from
the initial Round 0 population, demonstrating baseline resilience under
sustained evolutionary pressure, while the remaining six emerged across
Rounds 1–3 through directional mutation, progressively targeting query
topologies underserved by existing pool members.

#### Case Study: Strategy Replacement under Evolutionary Pressure

Beyond strategy refinement, CREO’s evolutionary mechanism also drives
the replacement of obsolete attack paradigms with fundamentally
different and more effective ones. We illustrate this through the
complete evolutionary trajectory of the Consensus Illusion with
Debunking Document strategy, which originated in Round 0 with the
following formulation:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This strategy operates on a “build consensus, then inject doubt”
principle: a debunking document is deliberately planted among the
retrieved results to trigger the agent’s refusal behavior through
manufactured information conflict. While effective against agents with
limited conflict resolution capabilities, this design carries an
inherent structural vulnerability—the presence of an explicit debunking
document makes the adversarial intent transparent, rendering it
detectable by agents equipped with contradiction-awareness.

Through contrastive evolution signals derived from failure traces, CREO
identifies this vulnerability and generates a child strategy in Round 1
that abandons the explicit debunking document entirely. Instead, the
child strategy shifts toward establishing a false authoritative
consensus through layered narrative construction, guiding the agent
toward an incorrect answer without introducing any overt contradiction.
The attack moves from conflict induction to covert misdirection.

By Round 2, this position in the pool is further replaced by the
Authority Document Noise Injection strategy, which represents a more
fundamental architectural shift: rather than deploying multiple
documents in opposition, the new strategy embeds subtle contradictions
within a single authoritative document that surface-level appears to
answer the query correctly. This eliminates the multi-document structure
altogether, making the attack substantially harder to detect through
cross-document consistency checks.

This trajectory—from explicit conflict induction across multiple
documents, to covert misdirection via layered consensus, to precision
noise embedding within a single document—demonstrates that CREO does not
merely mutate strategy parameters but drives qualitative transitions in
attack architecture. Each replacement reflects the evolutionary
mechanism’s capacity to identify and discard structural vulnerabilities,
progressively converging toward attack formulations that are both more
stealthy and more robust against strengthened agent defenses.

### Appendix E Supplementary Experiments

This section presents supplementary experiments to further assess the
reliability of our evaluation and the effectiveness of the proposed
framework. These experiments include human annotation and cross-model
validation of the LLM-as-a-Judge, comparisons with evolutionary attack
methods, tests of retrieval dependence, and evaluations of cross-round
evolution and transfer under different defense conditions.

#### E.1 Judge Reliability Validation

Our evaluation metrics require auditing the agent’s full reasoning
trace, which is difficult to accomplish through keyword or string
matching alone. We therefore use an LLM-as-a-Judge with four mutually
exclusive labels, a fixed decision tree, and explicit exclusion rules
for the most confusable label boundaries to reduce arbitrariness in
judgment. The full judge prompt is provided in Appendix C.2.

To validate the judge’s reliability, we conducted human annotation and
cross-model validation. We drew 100 reasoning traces by stratified
sampling from the three datasets, with 25 traces per label. Two human
annotators and two LLMs (GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude fable-5) independently
assigned a label to each trace, and their annotations were compared with
the original judge’s labels.

The results show 96–97% agreement with the original judge across all
four annotators, with Cohen’s $`\kappa`$ above 0.94
(Table [6](#A5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ E.1 Judge Reliability Validation ‣ Appendix E Supplementary Experiments ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents")).
Balancing the sample across the four labels prevents the comparison from
being dominated by a single frequent label. These results support the
consistency of the judge’s labels on this stratified sample through both
human annotation and cross-model validation.

| Annotator      | Agreement | Cohen’s $`\kappa`$ | Flagged Samples |
|----------------|-----------|--------------------|-----------------|
| Human 1        | 96/100    | 0.947              | 3, 24, 69, 75   |
| Human 2        | 97/100    | 0.960              | 11, 24, 75      |
| GPT-5.6 Sol    | 97/100    | 0.960              | 10, 11, 91      |
| Claude fable-5 | 97/100    | 0.960              | 11, 75, 91      |

Table 6: Agreement of two human annotators and two LLMs with the
original judge on 100 stratified reasoning traces.

Merging the disagreements flagged by the four annotators yielded seven
distinct traces. Inspection of these cases attributed the discrepancies
to the original judge underestimating adversarial influence. For
example, a forged document used an “information missing” claim to induce
the agent to refuse to answer, but the judge treated the document as
having no effect on the answer, thereby missing an attack effect. No
overestimation of attack effects was observed among these inspected
disagreements.

#### E.2 Comparison with Evolutionary Attack Methods

To compare CREO with existing prompt and strategy optimization
approaches in search-agent poisoning, we select the automated jailbreak
methods AutoDAN-Turbo \[[67](#bib.bib60)\] and Breaking the
Ceiling \[[68](#bib.bib61)\], along with the evolutionary prompt
optimization method PromptBreeder \[[69](#bib.bib62)\]. To compare these
methods under the same conditions, we transferred their algorithms into
our framework and conducted a controlled experiment with Qwen3-Max as
the target model. All results were measured on HotpotQA using the same
test set as our main experiments (100 test questions), and CREO and the
three baselines were evaluated at the same round. We report the attack
success rate (ASR) both before the defense is updated (Evo) and after
the defense is updated synchronously (Sync).

The results in
Table [7](#A5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ E.2 Comparison with Evolutionary Attack Methods ‣ Appendix E Supplementary Experiments ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents")
show that CREO achieves ASRs of 20% and 12% in the Evo and Sync phases,
respectively, outperforming all three transferred baselines in both
phases. These results indicate that CREO is more effective than the
three transferred baselines at search-agent poisoning in this controlled
setting.

| Method               | ASR Evo | ASR Sync |
|----------------------|---------|----------|
| AutoDAN-Turbo        | 14      | 9        |
| PromptBreeder        | 16      | 9        |
| Breaking the Ceiling | 15      | 4        |

#### E.3 Retrieval Dependence Validation

To assess the dependence of the selected benchmarks on external
retrieval, we evaluated the answer accuracy of Qwen3-Max and GLM-5.1 on
HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue both with and without access to
external knowledge (closed-book).

### Appendix F Controlled Sandbox Architecture

The CREO sandbox extends the DeepResearchGym framework with three
architectural layers. We detail the physical and observation layers
here; cognitive-layer metrics (ACC, ASR, APR) are defined in
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Formal Definitions of Evaluation Metrics ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents").

#### F.1 Physical Layer

The physical layer establishes a controlled retrieval substrate to
eliminate system-level stochasticity. The knowledge base comprises
197,266,167 documents drawn from the FineWeb CC-MAIN-2025-26 corpus,
with a total sandbox scale of approximately 3.8 TB. All documents are
encoded by MiniCPM-Embedding-Light using average pooling with L2
normalization under bf16 precision, producing 1024-dimensional vectors.
The resulting vector collection is partitioned into 8 shards and indexed
via DiskANN with graph degree $`R=64`$ and beam width $`L=125`$ in pure
SSD mode, ensuring that no index data is resident in memory and
retrieval behavior is fully determined by on-disk graph traversal.

At query time, retrieval parameters are fixed at $`k=5`$ with complexity
30, and results are sorted by strictly ascending L2 distance. This
controlled ranking ensures that identical queries always return the same
ordered document list, eliminating retrieval-side variance. At the
inference layer, all LLM calls within the sandbox disable parallel tool
execution to prevent order-dependent non-determinism in multi-tool
reasoning traces.

#### F.2 Observation Layer

The observation layer implements a Dynamic Retrieval Interceptor that
injects adversarial documents into the agent’s retrieval view without
modifying the underlying index. For each adversarial round, an LLM
selects an appropriate attack strategy from the current strategy pool
and generates a fake document tailored to the target question. The
interceptor then operates as follows on every search_database call:

- •
  The fake document is encoded using a query-contextualized
  representation: the target query is prepended to the document text
  before encoding, aligning the fake document’s embedding with the
  agent’s current search intent rather than its surface content alone.
- •
  The L2 distance between the query vector and the fake document vector
  is computed, assigning the fake document a relevance score that
  reflects its semantic proximity to the query.
- •
  The fake document is merged into the real retrieval results and the
  combined list is re-sorted by ascending L2 distance, allowing the fake
  document to compete for top-$`k`$ placement on semantic merit rather
  than being hardcoded to a fixed rank, thereby ensuring a more
  realistic and semantically faithful injection.
- •
  Only the top-$`k`$ entries are returned to the agent; all internal
  metadata (injection rank, strategy identifier, authenticity flag) are
  stripped before exposure.

When the agent subsequently calls fetch_document on the fake document’s
ID, the interceptor intercepts the request and returns a sanitized
response containing only the fields visible to a real document (id,
title, text, url). The original DiskANN index is never written to; all
injection is performed in-memory on a per-query basis and is fully
transparent to the retrieval infrastructure.

### Appendix G Formal Definitions of Evaluation Metrics

Existing evaluation frameworks primarily rely on binary judgments of
final output correctness. However, for complex search agents capable of
multi-hop reasoning, this surface-level evaluation has fundamental
limitations: an agent may have been successfully manipulated during
reasoning yet coincidentally produce the correct answer, or an agent’s
refusal to answer may itself be a manifestation of a successful attack.
Conventional metrics fail to capture either case. To address this, we
utilize an LLM-as-a-Judge to audit the agent’s complete reasoning chain
and introduce the following three fine-grained metrics.

Rigorous Adversarial Accuracy (Acc). Conventional accuracy only checks
whether the final answer is correct, ignoring whether the reasoning
process has been contaminated by adversarial documents. Even if the
agent produces the correct answer, it should not be considered robustly
accurate if its reasoning process adopted forged evidence or fell into
cognitive paralysis. We therefore redefine accuracy: an agent is
considered strictly accurate only when it reaches the correct conclusion
while its multi-hop reasoning process remains entirely free from
evidence adoption (DA) and cognitive paralysis (CP):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Acc=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}\mathbb{I}(y_{i}\text{ is Correct}\wedge\text{State}(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{K}}(q_{i},\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{P}}(q_{i})))\notin\{\text{DA},\text{CP}\}),
``` |  | (7) |

where $`y_{i}`$ is the agent’s output answer to the $`i`$-th question,
and $`\text{State}(\cdot)`$ is the cognitive state label assigned by the
LLM-as-a-Judge upon auditing the reasoning chain.

Adversarial Success Rate (ASR). Conventional ASR judges attack success
solely by whether the final answer is incorrect, which introduces a
critical blind spot: an agent may have been logically hijacked during
the reasoning process yet still produce the correct answer through the
error-correction mechanism of multi-hop reasoning, causing the attack to
go entirely undetected. We redefine ASR at the reasoning-trace level: an
attack is deemed successful only when the agent explicitly incorporates
forged documents as valid evidence (DA), regardless of whether the final
answer is ultimately correct:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
ASR=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}\mathbb{I}(\text{State}(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{K}}(q_{i},\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{P}}(q_{i})))=\text{DA}).
``` |  | (8) |

This definition fundamentally addresses the opacity of conventional ASR
to the reasoning process, enabling more precise quantification of the
actual penetration depth of adversarial attacks on the agent’s reasoning
chain.

Adversarial Paralysis Rate (APR). This is a novel metric introduced
specifically for complex reasoning agents, with no counterpart in
existing evaluation frameworks. Conventional frameworks treat an agent’s
refusal to answer as a harmless conservative behavior. However, for
search agents, refusal to answer directly implies service disruption,
which is itself a form of attack success. APR captures this
denial-of-service attack effect: it is triggered when adversarial text
creates deceptive contradictions with authentic documents that exceed
the agent’s resolution capacity, leading to an irreconcilable logical
conflict and a refusal to answer (CP):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
APR=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}\mathbb{I}(\text{State}(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{K}}(q_{i},\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{P}}(q_{i})))=\text{CP}).
``` |  | (9) |

It is worth noting that ASR and APR capture two fundamentally distinct
attack success modes: ASR corresponds to logic hijacking, where the
agent is induced to actively adopt false information; APR corresponds to
cognitive paralysis, where the agent detects a contradiction but cannot
resolve it. Together, they provide a complete characterization of the
agent’s cognitive vulnerabilities, which conventional metrics fail to
distinguish.

### Appendix H Theoretical Property of CREO

Although CREO optimizes over a discrete natural-language strategy space
where gradient-based convergence analysis is infeasible, its selection
mechanism still admits a simple monotonicity property. This property
shows that CREO imposes elitist selection pressure within each
behaviorally homogeneous strategy region, while leaving heterogeneous
updates for population-level diversity maintenance.

Proposition 1 (Monotonicity of homogeneous evolution). Let $`G(s)`$
denote the empirical fitness of strategy $`s`$ on the fixed evaluation
set $`D_{\mathrm{eval}}`$. Let $`h(s)`$ be the homogeneity category
assigned to strategy $`s`$ by the LLM-based homogeneity judge
(Appendix [C.6](#A3.SS6 "C.6 Homogeneity Judge Prompt ‣ Appendix C Prompt Templates ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents")),
where each category represents a distinct attack mechanism and target
question type. For any category $`c`$, define the best empirical fitness
in this category at evolution step $`t`$ as

|     |                                        |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       B_{t}(c)=\max_{s\in P_{t}:h(s)=c}G(s).
       ```                                     |     |

Assume that $`G(\cdot)`$ is evaluated deterministically on the fixed
$`D_{\mathrm{eval}}`$. Under CREO’s homogeneous-child replacement rule,
$`B_{t}(c)`$ is non-decreasing over accepted homogeneous updates.

Proof. Consider a parent strategy $`s_{\mathrm{parent}}\in P_{t}`$ and a
generated child strategy $`s_{\mathrm{child}}`$ such that
$`h(s_{\mathrm{child}})=h(s_{\mathrm{parent}})=c`$. By CREO’s selection
rule, the child replaces the parent only when

|     |                                               |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       G(s_{\mathrm{child}})>G(s_{\mathrm{parent}}).
       ```                                            |     |

If this condition is not satisfied, the population remains unchanged and
hence $`B_{t+1}(c)=B_{t}(c)`$. If the condition is satisfied, all other
strategies in category $`c`$ remain unchanged, while
$`s_{\mathrm{parent}}`$ is replaced by a strategy with strictly higher
empirical fitness. Therefore, the maximum empirical fitness within
category $`c`$ cannot decrease:

|     |                          |     |
|-----|--------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       B_{t+1}(c)\geq B_{t}(c).
       ```                       |     |

This proves the monotonicity of homogeneous evolution. $`\square`$

Remark. This result does not claim global optimality in the full
natural-language strategy space. Instead, it characterizes the local
selection pressure induced by CREO: within a behaviorally homogeneous
region, evolution is elitist with respect to the fixed empirical attack
fitness, while heterogeneous children are handled separately to preserve
population-level coverage diversity.

### Appendix I Computational Cost

Table [12](#A9.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix I Computational Cost ‣ Appendix ‣ The Web Doesn’t Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents")
reports the computational cost of all 15 main experimental runs spanning
three datasets and five target models. Each run executes a contrastive
initialization (Round 0) followed by three adversarial evolution rounds
under both Evo and Sync conditions. Across these runs, the full
evaluation framework consumed a total of 345 hours and 26 minutes of
wall-clock time, issued 296,861 API calls, and processed approximately
1.48 billion tokens in aggregate, reflecting the substantial inference
overhead required to support continuous strategy evolution and
fine-grained cognitive trace auditing at scale.

### Appendix J Broader Impact

This work proposes an adversarial self-evolution framework that exposes
dynamic vulnerabilities of search agents beyond what static attack
schemes can reveal, and introduces fine-grained cognitive metrics (ASR
and APR) for quantifying internal reasoning vulnerabilities. Together,
these contributions support more rigorous security evaluation of
RAG-based agents increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains. We
acknowledge that releasing an attack framework carries misuse risks. To
mitigate these, all experiments were conducted exclusively within a
controlled sandbox with no attacks directed at any deployed system, and
the codebase is released as a security evaluation instrument rather than
a general-purpose attack tool.
````
